fields.definition: A monitoring feed or dedicated receiver that reproduces a station's actual off-air signal, letting staff hear the program exactly as the audience does, after all processing, encoding, and transmission delay.
fields.plain_english: A speaker or radio that plays back what the station is really sending out. It lets the crew hear just what people at home hear, after all the gear has done its job.
fields.purpose_function: It confirms the station is on the air and that the signal still sounds right after processing and transmission, catching dead air, distortion, or the wrong content.
fields.practical_application: An engineer or host keeps the air monitor up to verify the broadcast and to spot faults before listeners call in to complain.
common_mistakes: Assuming the console output matches the air signal, ignoring processing and transmission delay
Confusing the air monitor with the console monitor feed
Turning the air monitor off during a shift and missing dead air or an outage
scenario_contexts: An engineer verifying the transmitter is passing clean audio
A host checking that a recorded spot actually aired
Troubleshooting distortion heard by listeners but not on the console

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: The microphone used by on-air talent (announcer, host, or DJ) to deliver spoken program audio; in radio it is typically a large-diaphragm cardioid dynamic mic chosen for a warm, present voice and strong rejection of room noise.
fields.plain_english: The mic the on-air host talks into. It is usually a tough dynamic mic that makes the voice sound full and blocks out room noise.
fields.purpose_function: It captures the presenter's voice at broadcast quality while rejecting background noise and handling close, loud speech without popping or distortion.
fields.practical_application: Engineers mount it on a shock-mounted boom arm with a pop filter, set it a few inches from the mouth, and route it through a mic processor before the console.
common_mistakes: Working too far from the mic, which raises room noise and lowers voice level
Skipping the pop filter, so plosives cause loud popping
Setting gain too high and clipping loud speech
Treating a rugged dynamic mic like a fragile condenser and vice versa
scenario_contexts: A morning-show host speaking live on a music station
A sportscaster calling play-by-play from a booth
Voice-tracking pre-recorded segments for later airing
A news reader delivering a live top-of-hour bulletin

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A recording of a station's actual broadcast output, captured for later review, talent critique, compliance logging, or as a demo of on-air work.
fields.plain_english: A recording of what a station actually put on the air. People use it to review how a show sounded or to prove what was broadcast.
fields.purpose_function: It documents exactly what went out over the air so managers can coach talent, confirm content ran, and meet legal logging rules.
fields.practical_application: A host saves an aircheck of their shift to build a demo, while engineers keep automated airchecks to settle complaints and provide regulatory proof.
common_mistakes: Recording the console feed instead of the true off-air signal, missing processing changes
Not logging continuously and losing proof of what aired
Confusing an edited demo aircheck with an unedited compliance log
scenario_contexts: A DJ compiling a demo reel from recent shows
Reviewing a broadcast after a listener complaint
Keeping a legal log of everything transmitted

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A device or software system that automatically records a station's on-air signal, often as a continuous logging recorder or as a skimmer that captures only the mic-open talk segments.
fields.plain_english: A machine or program that records what the station broadcasts, usually all day long. Some versions only save the parts where the host is talking.
fields.purpose_function: It provides an automatic archive of the broadcast for legal logging, complaint resolution, and reviewing talent performance without anyone hitting record.
fields.practical_application: Engineers feed it the off-air or console output; a skimmer mode triggered by the mic switch stores short talk breaks so a host can grab an aircheck quickly.
common_mistakes: Feeding it a pre-processing source, so the log does not match the true air signal
Letting the storage fill and overwrite required legal logs
Assuming skimmer mode captured everything when it only records mic-open segments
scenario_contexts: Maintaining a 24-hour legal log of the broadcast
A host retrieving a talk-break aircheck for a demo
Pulling archived audio after a compliance query

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A small, acoustically treated room built for a presenter to record or broadcast voice, isolated from control-room and studio noise so speech is captured cleanly.
fields.plain_english: A small, sound-treated room where the announcer talks into the mic. It is quiet and isolated so the voice is recorded clearly.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the announcer a quiet, low-reflection space so the microphone picks up a clean, dry voice free of room echo and outside noise.
fields.practical_application: A technician sets up the talent mic, headphones, and a talkback link inside the booth, then treats the walls to cut reflections and seals the door for isolation.
common_mistakes: Assuming any small room is dead enough without acoustic treatment
Leaving noisy fans or computers inside the booth
Poor door sealing that lets control-room sound leak into the mic
scenario_contexts: Recording station voice-overs and imaging
A news anchor reading live from an isolated booth
Tracking narration for a documentary or promo

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A dedicated audio feed carrying the on-air announcer's voice, routed separately from music and other program elements so it can be mixed, distributed, or sent to remote sites on its own.
fields.plain_english: A separate audio path that carries just the announcer's voice. Keeping it on its own makes it easy to mix or send it where it is needed.
fields.purpose_function: It isolates the announcer's voice as a discrete signal so it can be balanced against program audio, recorded alone, or delivered to another site or network.
fields.practical_application: An engineer splits the talent mic to a dedicated bus, then routes that announcer feed to the console, a remote codec, or a separate recorder.
common_mistakes: Confusing the announcer feed with a full program mix that already includes music
Sending a feed with the announcer's own return audio, causing echo instead of a clean mix-minus
Not labeling routing, so the wrong source reaches a remote site
scenario_contexts: Feeding an announcer's voice to a remote sports venue
Routing a clean voice track to a separate recorder
Sending narration to another studio for a shared broadcast

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A set of microphones arranged to capture audience sound, such as applause, laughter, and crowd ambience, during a broadcast or recorded event, then mixed in to convey atmosphere.
fields.plain_english: A group of mics aimed at the crowd to pick up clapping, laughter, and general noise. The sound is mixed in so the show feels live.
fields.purpose_function: It captures the room's reaction and ambience so the broadcast sounds live and energetic instead of dry, while keeping crowd noise controllable in the mix.
fields.practical_application: A technician places several mics around the seating, balances their levels to avoid feedback and harshness, and rides the crowd level up during applause.
common_mistakes: Placing mics where they pick up the PA and feed back
Leaving crowd mics wide open, raising the noise floor between reactions
Too few mics for the space, giving thin or uneven audience sound
scenario_contexts: Broadcasting a live comedy or game show
Covering a sports event to capture crowd reaction
A live concert broadcast that needs audience ambience

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: An audio codec, in hardware or software, that encodes and transports high-quality contribution audio, meaning program material sent from a remote site back to the studio or network, typically over IP, ISDN, or dedicated links with an emphasis on quality and low latency.
fields.plain_english: A box or program that squeezes high-quality audio so it can travel from a remote spot back to the studio. It aims for great sound and little delay, not just small file size.
fields.purpose_function: It carries program-grade audio between locations reliably and with low delay, so remote broadcasts sound as good as studio audio while using available network links.
fields.practical_application: An engineer connects the codec at a remote venue over IP or ISDN, sets a codec algorithm and bit rate, and monitors latency and dropouts across the link.
common_mistakes: Confusing contribution links with lower-quality distribution codecs
Choosing a low-latency setting without enough network headroom, causing dropouts
Ignoring buffer and jitter settings, so audio glitches over IP
scenario_contexts: Sending a reporter's audio from the field to the studio
Linking two studios for a shared program
Backhauling a live remote concert to the broadcast center

sources: EBU technical documentation (audio contribution over IP)

fields.definition: The room in a broadcast facility that houses the main mixing console and audio processing and routing gear, where an operator mixes and controls all program audio for a studio or on-air channel.
fields.plain_english: The room with the main mixing desk where an operator controls all the sound for a show. It is where the audio for the broadcast is put together.
fields.purpose_function: It centralizes mixing, monitoring, and routing so one operator can combine mics, playback, and remote feeds into the finished program audio.
fields.practical_application: An engineer works the console here to balance talent mics, music, and remote sources, monitor the air signal, and send the mix on down the air chain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the audio control room with the on-air studio or talent booth
Poor monitor calibration, so mixes sound wrong on the air
Cluttered routing labels that cause the wrong source to go to air
scenario_contexts: Operating the console for a live radio show
Mixing a live sports broadcast from the control room
Routing and monitoring remote feeds during a special broadcast

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)
